newsitem.title: FRANCE: Big Eurotunnel investor backs debt plan.
newsitem.headline: Big Eurotunnel investor backs debt plan.

text.p: Embattled Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel SA /Plc said on Monday that a big U.S. investor which had opposed a debt rescue plan would now vote in favour of the make-or-break refinancing deal.

The news was a breakthrough for Eurotunnel executive chairman Patrick Ponsolle who has warned that rejection of the restructuring of its 70 billion francs in bank debt would lead to bankrupcty and be a "collective suicide" by investors.
The company said in a statement U.S fund manager Northern Cross Investments would vote its shares in support of the debt plan to be put to shareholders on July 10.

"Patrick Ponsolle, executive chairman of the Eurotunnel group, has been informed that the 36.66 million voting rights held by funds managed by Northern Cross Investments will vote in favour of the Eurotunnel board's financial restructuring plan at the next shareholders meeting," the company said in a statement.
The change of heart came after Ponsolle flew to Boston last Thursday to meet a Northern Cross fund manager to explain the restructuring proposals, sources close to Eurotunnel said.

French lawyer Sophie L'Helias, head of proxy vote-holder Franklin Global Investor Services (FGIS), earlier told Reuters that a shareholder owning around 38 million shares had changed its voting position and would vote for the restructuring plan.
A Eurotunnel spokeswoman confirmed the investor was Northern Cross and that it held three percent of the company's capital, despite the different numbers used for the share holding.

Northern Cross, along with other institutional investors represented by L'Helias, had said it would vote against the debt plan unless the banks cancelled a quarter of the debt and dropped a "substitution clause" which allows them to put in new management.
Apart from Northern Cross those other investors were still opposed to the plan and would vote against the restructuring unless their conditions were met, L'Helias said.
A second Eurotunnel spokeswoman said, "This shows that a professional and rational investor who studies the plan can only conclude this is the best possible solution."
In addition to the institutional proxies held by L'Helias, two French small shareholders' associations are also threatening to vote against the debt deal if the terms are not sweetened.
A key demand is for an extension to the operating licence which runs out in 2052.

The French and British governments declined to comment on Ponsolle's interview with the Financial Times in which he said Paris and London both want a share of future profits in exchange for an extension.

A Eurotunnel statement quoted Ponsolle as saying, "We have a fair chance to know in the days to come if the two governments are accepting this request of the company." The statement added, however, "I don't have the habit of selling the bear's skin before the bear is caught."
Eurotunnel needs a two-thirds majority of French shareholders and 75 percent of British investors to approve the debt pact with its 174 lenders. About 600,000 investors are French.
